rich_summary: This section recounts how the river goddess Ganga becomes the wife of King Santanu of the Kuru line. Earlier, a celestial maiden had promised King Pratipa that she would marry his son; Pratipa later instructs Santanu to accept her without questioning her actions or origins. When Santanu meets the radiant maiden by the Ganges, he asks her to marry him. She agrees on one strict condition: he must never question or interfere with anything she does. Santanu accepts, and they live happily together. However, each time a child is born, Ganga throws the newborn into the river, claiming it is for the king’s good. Bound by his promise, Santanu remains silent through seven such deaths. When she attempts to drown the eighth child, he finally protests, breaking the pact. Ganga then reveals her divine identity and the cosmic purpose behind the events.

highlight_spans.why: Pratipa's declaration reframes the celestial maiden not as a lover but as a future daughter‑in‑law, setting the prophetic foundation for Santanu's marriage.
The maiden’s crucial condition—Santanu must never question or interfere with her actions—creates the moral tension that drives the tragedy of their children.
The shocking sequence in which Ganga casts each newborn into the river embodies the emotional and ethical conflict of Santanu’s vow versus his paternal grief.
Santanu finally breaks his silence to save the eighth child, the pivotal moment that ends the divine marriage and leads to Ganga’s revelation.

top_scenes.scene_text: King Santanu first beholds the radiant maiden on the banks of the Ganges, her celestial ornaments gleaming as the river glows behind her.
Under moonlit waters of the Ganges, Ganga calmly releases a newborn child into the river while Santanu watches in silent anguish.
Santanu desperately reaches out to stop Ganga as she prepares to cast the eighth child into the river, breaking his vow at last.
